title: Sergio Ramos-led consortium’s Sevilla takeover talks break down
content:
A Sergio Ramos-led consortium’s proposed deal to buy Sevilla appears to have collapsed.

The Athletic reported on May 12 that the consortium, led by the 40-year-old former Real Madrid defender, had reached an agreement in principle to buy the Spanish club in a deal worth around €444million. However, talks have broken down after differences emerged between the parties and sources close to the selling side consider the negotiations to be off.

Sources close to Ramos left the latest meeting with the impression that the deal is now difficult to conclude and are awaiting formal communication that it is off, although they understand this is unlikely to arrive before the exclusivity deadline of May 31.

After several meetings between the two parties over the last two weeks, another meeting took place on Wednesday in which Ramos’s team presented a new offer and changed the terms of the initial proposal under which a preliminary agreement had been reached.

In the new offer, Ramos, together with fund Five Eleven and a group of Mexican investors, proposed buying a smaller stake in stages while contributing more money through a capital increase.

The new proposal involved a smaller offer up front, but the equity value was higher, according to sources close to the bid.

The terms of the initial agreement in principle reached this month involved the Ramos-backed consortium acquiring 85 per cent of the club’s shares for €275m, while also assuming €85m in debt and committing to an €80m capital increase.

However, according to Sevilla sources the new proposal involved a reduced initial offer of €100m for 18 per cent of the club’s shares. This structure would leave the rest of Sevilla’s shareholders — holders of roughly 54,000 shares — outside the transaction.

The consortium would then gradually increase its stake to 60 per cent through capital increase: initially €120m to take the stake to 42 per cent — and a controlling position of the club — before pushing through further capital increase.

According to sources close to Ramos, the new proposal would total €335m and would be structured as follows: €120m in a capital increase, €133m paid directly to shareholders, and €82m in deferred payments to shareholders. This would mean they are effectively putting in €192.6m for 60 per cent of the club’s equity value (excluding debt), proportionally above the €272.85m previously proposed for 85 per cent of the club’s equity value (also excluding debt). Ramos’ bid also had the backing of the bank Santander, according to sources briefed on the situation.

Sources within La Liga who are familiar with the situation say that the €120m figure would approximately correspond to the club’s losses over the last four years. That capital increase would rebalance the club’s accounts and significantly improve its financial fair play position.

Members of the bidding group were reconsidering their position due to changes in the terms of the deal and a growing feeling that the process was dragging on as the exclusivity deadline approaches.

Shareholders also had doubts over the new proposal as they felt it was not backed by half of the required guarantees and believed that there was still a lack of certainty. Sources close to Ramos deny this.

Sources on both sides left the latest meeting with the feeling that the situation would be very difficult to salvage, given the lack of time. Sources close to the shareholders also felt the new proposal was not consistent because it represented a step down from the initial offer. Ramos’ side argue the offer is worth more as a proportion.

Sevilla, meanwhile, are already considering another takeover proposal. Ramos is considering holding a press conference after the exclusivity deadline to explain the situation.

Ramos is the public face of a group backed by the Five Eleven fund that entered a three-month period of exclusivity to acquire the Spanish side in January.

The former Spain defender progressed through the academy at Sevilla and made his first-team debut in February 2004. He returned to the club in 2023 following 16 years at Madrid and two seasons at Paris Saint-Germain.

The 2010 World Cup winner made 87 appearances for Sevilla during his two spells at the club and has been a free agent since leaving Mexican club Monterrey in December.
